An HTTP cache stores response bodies and metadata, such as status and headers, so a later GET can reuse them. The browser's private cache serves that one user agent. A CDN runs shared caches at edge servers near users. The origin is the server responsible for the logo. A hit reuses a stored response that is suitable for this request. A miss means there is no stored response usable for this request.

With empty caches, the GET goes browser, then CDN, then origin. The response returns origin, then CDN, then browser. Each cache stores it only if its policy permits. What is stored is the HTTP response, not a replicated database record. The origin may read a database, but a later hit need not reach the database. Not every request reaches the origin.

A browser hit serves the logo from that browser's private cache and avoids the network request, so it does not reach the CDN or the origin. After another browser misses locally, a CDN hit can return the logo from the shared edge without contacting the origin.

Request hit ratio is cache hits divided by requests at a specified layer. Here the layer is this CDN, and a CDN hit means serving from its cache without contacting origin. Of the 1,000 GETs that reach the CDN, 800 are hits, so the ratio is 800 / 1,000 = 80%. Each of the other 200 requests makes exactly one origin request, and there are no background requests or extra layers, so origin receives 200 requests.

That 80% does not include browser hits, because those never entered this denominator. It is not a byte hit ratio, because response sizes differ. Revalidation, background refreshes, extra layers, and application work need their own measurements. 80% does not prove 80% less database work or 80% less transfer.

Repeated public assets and popular published pages can reduce latency by answering nearby and can reduce origin requests and transfer. CDN requests and transfer can incur charges, and key configuration, invalidation, and monitoring add operational work. For a low-traffic Notes app whose responses are mostly private or rarely reused, omit shared caching if those measured benefits do not justify the cost. Compare reuse, latency, and total cost, and keep private notes private rather than sharing them to raise the hit ratio.

Cache-Control carries caching directives. public explicitly permits shared caching, subject to other rules. max-age sets the freshness lifetime in seconds; here it is 60, and the browser uses that. s-maxage overrides max-age only in shared caches, so the CDN uses 300 seconds. A fresh response is young enough to reuse without validation under its policy. A stale response has reached its freshness limit; the body need not be deleted. Freshness is permission to reuse, not proof that the origin page is unchanged. Age estimates seconds since the response was generated or successfully validated at the origin, including time already spent in caches.

This response arrives with Age: 90. Ignore transit and clock differences. The browser's lifetime is 60 seconds, so the browser is 30 seconds past its lifetime and must not treat the response as fresh. The CDN's shared lifetime is 300 seconds, so it has 300 − 90 = 210 seconds of freshness left and may treat the response as fresh. Receiving the response does not start a new full lifetime.

Later the CDN holds a stale published page with ETag: "v1" and its policy does not allow serving that stale. A representation is the returned form of the resource, such as the page HTML. Revalidation checks whether the stored representation is still usable. An ETag is an opaque validator for that representation; the client keeps the tag and does not interpret it. The CDN sends a conditional GET to origin with If-None-Match: "v1", asking for a body only if the selected representation no longer matches.

If the page is unchanged, origin returns 304 Not Modified and no replacement body. The CDN updates its stored metadata, including freshness, and answers the browser's ordinary GET with the body it already kept, the v1 body.

If the page is now v2, origin returns 200 with the new body and its validator, ETag: "v2". The CDN replaces its stored representation if policy allows, and serves that new body. The ETag does not push the change into other caches.

Validation does not avoid the network request. Origin was contacted. A 304 only saves retransmitting the body on that hop. Origin may still run application logic or query a database to decide whether the representation changed, so validation does not guarantee that no origin or database work happened.

evidence.quote: Cache-Control is a response header carrying caching rules called directives. A fresh response is young enough for reuse without validation under its policy. A stale response has reached its freshness limit; its body need not be deleted. Freshness is permission to reuse, not proof that origin content is unchanged.

For a public published Notes page, consider Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, s-maxage=300. public explicitly permits shared caching subject to other rules. max-age sets the freshness lifetime in seconds. s-maxage overrides it only in shared caches; the browser still uses 60 seconds.

Age estimates seconds since generation or successful validation at origin, including time spent through caches. If this response arrives with Age: 90, ignoring transit and clock differences, the browser is 30 seconds past its lifetime. The CDN has 300 − 90 = 210 seconds of freshness left. Receiving it does not start a new full lifetime.

A representation is the returned form of a resource, such as a published note's HTML. Revalidation checks whether the stored representation remains usable. ETag is an opaque validator identifying that representation; clients preserve the tag rather than interpreting it.

The CDN has a stale page with ETag: "v1" and cannot serve it stale under its policy. It sends a conditional GET to origin with If-None-Match: "v1", asking for the body only if the selected representation no longer matches.

If unchanged, origin returns 304 Not Modified without a replacement body. The CDN updates applicable stored metadata, including freshness information, and uses its retained body to answer the browser's ordinary GET.

If changed, origin returns 200 with the new body and its validator, for example ETag: "v2". The CDN replaces its stored representation if policy allows. An ETag does not push changes into other caches.
304 saves retransmitting the body across the validation hop. Origin was still contacted and may run application logic or query a database to decide whether the representation changed.

Cookies are state held by the browser. Set-Cookie asks the browser to store that state. Cookie sends it back on a later request. Authorization is a request header that carries credentials. Authentication establishes who the caller is. Authorization checks whether that caller may read the note.

no-cache, used without extra qualifiers, allows storage but requires successful validation before every reuse. It does not mean never store. private forbids shared-cache storage. It does not forbid browser storage, and it does not by itself require validation on every use. no-store tells HTTP caches not to store the response. It does not erase copies already delivered, and it does not replace a permission check.

For a public page that may be stored but must be validated before every reuse, use unqualified no-cache. For a private note that may live only in the browser cache, use private. For a sensitive note that HTTP caches must not store, use no-store. Other directives can still apply, and the policy has to be chosen explicitly.

Cookie, Set-Cookie, and authentication are not a universal per-user cache key and not a guarantee that the CDN will skip the response. They do not automatically create a separate cache entry per user or universally prevent caching. Requests that carry Authorization have special shared-cache restrictions, but the response policy can still permit reuse. A shared response reused for the wrong user can leak a private note.

Keep the permission check at the origin. For private-note routes, verify that the explicit private or no-store policy and the actual CDN rules prevent shared storage and reuse. Test with different users. Do not mark a personalized note public to raise the hit rate.

evidence.quote: Cookies are browser-held state: Set-Cookie asks the browser to store it; Cookie sends it back. Authorization is a request header carrying credentials. Authentication establishes identity; authorization checks permission to read a note.

For a public page, unqualified no-cache allows storage but requires successful validation before every reuse. It does not mean never store. For a private note where browser storage is acceptable, private forbids shared-cache storage; it neither forbids browser storage nor requires validation on every use. Other directives still apply.

For a sensitive note, no-store instructs HTTP caches not to store the response. It cannot erase previously delivered copies or replace permission checks. Choose the policy explicitly instead of relying on a header's misleading name.

A shared response reused for the wrong user can leak private notes. Cookie and Set-Cookie do not automatically create per-user cache entries or universally prevent caching. Authorization-bearing requests have special shared-cache restrictions, but response policy can permit reuse; authentication alone is no universal CDN bypass guarantee.

Keep authorization at origin. For private-note routes, verify that explicit private/no-store policies and actual CDN rules prevent shared storage and reuse. Test different users; do not mark personalized notes public for a higher hit rate.
no-cache means validate; no-store means do not store; private excludes shared caches.

A cache key identifies which stored response can satisfy a request. HTTP caching uses the method and the target URL, and selected request headers distinguish variants. A variant is a different returned form of the same resource.

This export changes with the query, ?format=pdf versus ?format=html, and with Accept-Language, en versus fr. The format values have to stay distinct in the key. If the CDN is configured to ignore query parameters, it could return HTML for a PDF request. Verify the actual key settings. Do not assume every CDN includes every query parameter. Vary: Accept-Language tells a cache that this request header's value must match before the stored response is reused, which separates the language variants when the cache supports and honors Vary. CDN support and custom keys differ, so verify that both format and language survive the real matching rules, or bypass caching until they do.

Dropping a distinction that changes the body returns the wrong variant, such as HTML for a PDF request or English for a French request. Keeping irrelevant tracking parameters does the opposite harm to the hit rate: they create extra cache entries and fewer hits. Exclude a parameter only after confirming it does not change the response.

Vary does not authorize sharing private notes. It does not change the URL, grant permission, or override private or no-store. Separating public variants is not permission to share a private note.

evidence.quote: A cache key identifies which stored response can satisfy a request. HTTP caching uses the method and target URL, with selected request headers distinguishing variants: different returned forms of the same resource.

Our public Notes export varies by ?format=pdf versus ?format=html, and Accept-Language: en versus fr. Keep the format query values distinct. A CDN configured to ignore them could return HTML for a PDF request; verify the actual key settings rather than assuming every CDN includes every query parameter.

Vary: Accept-Language tells a cache that this request header's value must match for reuse. It separates language variants when supported and honored. CDN support and custom keys differ: verify that both format and language survive the actual matching rules, or bypass caching until they do.

Irrelevant tracking parameters can create extra entries and fewer hits. Exclude them only after confirming they do not change the response. Vary does not change the URL, grant permission or override private/no-store. Correctly separated public variants are not permission to share private notes.
Keep distinctions that change content; remove only distinctions proven irrelevant.

A versioned asset URL changes when the bytes change. Publish app.v2.js instead of overwriting app.v1.js. Long caching fits those immutable URLs, because the bytes at each URL stay the same. The page that refers to the script must be updated to request v2. An old cached copy of the page can still request v1, so v1 has to remain available for those clients until that page reference has moved.

A CDN purge removes or invalidates the targeted CDN entries according to the provider. Verify that it covers the relevant URLs, variants, and CDN cache layers, and check how it propagates and when it completes. Purge is something to check, not a simultaneous replacement everywhere.

The edited page that keeps the same URL needs a freshness or revalidation policy chosen for the update delay you can tolerate. A database edit does not rewrite stored HTTP responses. Short freshness, or validation on each reuse, is a different trade-off from a long-lived versioned file.

A database update or a CDN purge does not instantly update every browser. Purging CDN entries does not evict fresh browser copies or erase content already downloaded. Unpublishing can stop future origin access and can trigger purges, but a public page already delivered cannot be instantly revoked. Choose the lifetimes with that limit in mind before publishing.

evidence.quote: A versioned asset URL changes when its bytes change: publish app.v2.js instead of overwriting app.v1.js. Long caching fits immutable assets, whose bytes stay unchanged at each URL. Update the referring page to request v2; an old cached page can still ask for v1.

A published note that keeps its URL needs a chosen freshness/revalidation policy matching the tolerated update delay. A database edit does not rewrite stored HTTP responses. Short freshness or validation on each reuse makes a different trade-off from long-lived versioned assets.

A CDN purge removes or invalidates targeted CDN entries according to the provider. Verify coverage of the relevant URLs, variants and CDN cache layers, plus propagation and completion behavior. Purge is an operation to check, not an assumption of simultaneous replacement everywhere.

Purging CDN entries does not evict fresh browser copies or erase downloaded content. Unpublishing can stop future origin access and trigger purges, but already delivered public content cannot be instantly revoked. Choose cache lifetimes with that limit in mind before publishing.

stale-while-revalidate permits a bounded reuse of a stale response while the cache attempts validation in the background, which hides that validation latency. stale-if-error permits a bounded stale fallback when an eligible error happens, such as an origin failure. Both are optional permissions. They are not a promise that the response is fresh or that the origin is available. Assume this cache supports them, has an eligible stored response, has no conflicting directive, and transit time is negligible.

The response is fresh for 60 seconds. The stale windows start when that freshness expires. At age 75 it is 15 seconds stale. The extra 30-second stale-while-revalidate window permits reuse while a background revalidation runs, through age 90.

At age 150, with an eligible origin error, the response is 90 seconds stale. Freshness ended at 60 seconds, and stale-if-error lasts another 120 seconds, through age 180. Age 150 is inside that window, so the stored copy may be served as the error fallback.

At age 200 with the same error, neither extension still applies. The background-validation window ended at age 90, and the error window ended at age 180. These directives do not authorize stale reuse.

If no stored copy exists, a cold cache has nothing to fall back to, and an exhausted allowance can expose the failure. This policy is unsuitable for a private note or for urgent removal. Stale reuse can keep serving the old response, these directives do not override private or no-store, and private-note correctness or an urgent takedown can forbid stale reuse even when it would help a public help page stay available.

evidence.quote: stale-while-revalidate permits bounded stale reuse while attempting background validation, hiding validation latency. stale-if-error permits bounded stale fallback on eligible errors, such as an origin failure. These are optional permissions, not freshness or availability promises.

Consider Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=30, stale-if-error=120. Assume cache support, an eligible stored response, no conflicting policy and negligible transit time. The response is fresh for 60 seconds; stale windows start when freshness expires.

At age 75 it is 15 seconds stale: the additional 30-second background-validation window permits reuse while refreshing, through age 90. At age 150 with an eligible error, it is 90 seconds stale: the error allowance lasts another 120 seconds after expiry, through age 180. At age 200 neither extension still permits stale reuse.

A cold cache has no response to fall back to, and exhausted allowances can expose the failure. Verify provider support and policy; these directives do not override private/no-store. Private-note correctness or urgent removal may forbid stale reuse even when it improves public-help availability.
Count stale allowance after freshness expires, and require an eligible stored copy.
